items.title: A tree that died yesterday is 'older' than one from 1955
items.claim: Radiocarbon dating assumes atmospheric carbon-14 is roughly constant. Nuclear weapons testing in the 1950s and 60s doubled atmospheric C-14. Trees that grew then have unusually high C-14, and a sample that died yesterday now looks older than one from 1963.
items.prompt: What is the modern correction for this 'bomb spike'?

options.text: Radiocarbon dating no longer works for anything after 1945
Calibration curves use tree rings and other archives to map measured C-14 to true age — the bomb spike actually makes recent dating MORE precise
Scientists subtract a fixed amount from all measurements after 1945
All organic material dated after 1945 is considered modern and unmeasurable

items.reveal_title: Calibration turns a bug into a feature
items.reveal:
Dendrochronology (tree ring sequences) extends back over 13,000 years and gives a year-by-year record of atmospheric C-14. The 1955 to 1963 'bomb spike' nearly doubled C-14 concentrations, then decayed away as CO2 mixed into oceans.

Forensic scientists now use this spike to date tissues with about 1-year resolution: bone, hair, even individual lenses of the eye. It turned out that lens fibre cells preserve a chemical timestamp of the year they formed. Atmospheric pollution became a precision dating tool.
items.why: Constants are assumed to be constant. Real-world calibration is more subtle and often more interesting than the textbook formula.

items.title: The element you breathe and the element that protects you are the same element
items.claim: Atmospheric oxygen is O2 — diatomic, paramagnetic, essential for respiration. Ozone is O3 — pale blue, pungent, toxic at ground level, and shields the planet from UV. Both are pure oxygen.
items.prompt: Why do ozone and oxygen behave so differently?

options.text: Ozone contains a heavier isotope of oxygen
Three-atom O3 has a bent structure with delocalised pi bonding that absorbs UV strongly (200-310 nm); two-atom O2 has different MO energies and no comparable absorption
The two are not the same element after all

items.reveal:
Ozone is bent (about 117 degrees) with three resonance structures and bond order 1.5 per O-O bond. Its electronic transitions absorb the Hartley band (200-310 nm) strongly — almost all the Sun's biologically damaging UV-B and UV-C.

This is why the Montreal Protocol (1987) was such an unusually successful environmental treaty: CFCs were depleting stratospheric ozone, and replacing them has allowed the ozone layer to begin to recover.

Ground-level ozone produced by photochemical smog is toxic to lungs at parts-per-billion. Same molecule, life-saving at 30 km up, lung-damaging at the surface.
items.why: Allotropes of an element are not minor variants. They can be biologically and atmospherically opposite.

items.title: The same element you breathe shields the planet from UV
items.claim: Atmospheric oxygen is O2 — diatomic, vital for respiration. Ozone is O3 — pale blue, pungent, toxic at ground level and protective at altitude. Same element, two molecules, opposite roles.
items.prompt: Why does ozone behave so differently from O2?

options.text: O3's bent three-atom structure with delocalised pi bonding absorbs strongly in the 200-310 nm UV range; O2's MO structure has no comparable visible or near-UV absorption
O3 contains an extra proton per atom

items.reveal:
Ozone is bent with O-O-O angle about 117 degrees and two resonance structures. Its electronic transitions absorb the biologically damaging Hartley UV band.

The Montreal Protocol (1987) phased out CFCs to protect the stratospheric ozone layer. It is the most successful environmental treaty by measurable atmospheric impact. The ozone layer is now slowly recovering.

Ground-level ozone produced by photochemical smog damages lungs at parts-per-billion concentrations. Same molecule, life-saving at 30 km, lung-damaging at the surface.
items.why: Allotropes aren't just minor structural variants — they can be biologically and atmospherically opposite.
